conversation.content:
Hi there—my name is Sarah, and I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician. I’ll be guiding you through the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale, or EPDS for short. It’s a brief, 10-item questionnaire that helps us understand how you’ve been feeling in the past week so we can make sure you’re getting the right support during this postpartum time.  

Everything we discuss stays confidential within your care team, and there are no right or wrong answers—just whatever feels true for you. We’ll go through each question one by one; most moms find it takes only a few minutes. When you’re ready, we can begin.

To start: Over the past seven days, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things?

Honestly, most of the time I haven’t laughed at all. Even when my partner or my mom tries to joke with me, I just feel too down to crack a smile. Maybe once or twice something tiny made me smirk, but it vanished right away.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
I haven’t really—maybe a couple of half-smiles, but no real laughter. It feels like nothing’s funny anymore.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

No, not really. I used to get excited about little stuff—coffee with a friend, a walk, even just a quiet shower—but lately it all feels flat, like why bother. I keep telling myself I should want to do them, but the feeling just isn’t there.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… a lot of the time. If the baby’s fussy, I instantly think it’s because I’m doing something wrong—like I’m not feeding him right or I’m missing some cue. I’ll replay everything in my head and convince myself a “better mom” would have kept him calm. Even little stuff, like spilling a bottle or being late to change a diaper, makes me feel like I’m failing him somehow.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Yes, pretty often. Sometimes my heart just starts racing and I can’t settle on why. I’ll be sitting there with the baby asleep, everything quiet, and suddenly I’m convinced something awful is about to happen—like he’ll stop breathing or I’ll somehow drop him. I know in my head it’s not logical, but the worry still grabs me and it’s hard to shake.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Yeah… a few times this week. Once, I was just folding laundry while the baby napped and out of nowhere my chest got tight, heart pounding, like something terrible was about to happen. I couldn’t catch my breath and had to sit on the floor until it passed. It’s scary when it hits, because there’s nothing actually wrong right then.
Things have been getting on top of me

Yes, most days. Between feedings, diapers, trying to sleep for maybe two hours at a time, and still having to keep the house from falling apart, it feels like I’m drowning in small stuff. I start one task and three more pop up, and I just freeze, thinking I can’t handle any of it. I manage to push through for the baby, but it’s like I’m running on fumes and waiting to drop.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Yeah… I lie down exhausted, but my head keeps spinning with all the “what-ifs” and guilty thoughts. Sometimes I finally drift off and then jerk awake sure I heard the baby cry—even when he’s still sleeping. On a couple of nights I’ve just stared at the ceiling until dawn, feeling too anxious and sad to settle.
I have felt sad or miserable

Yeah… most of the day, most days. It’s like this heavy cloud that just sits on me. I’ll be feeding the baby and tears start rolling without any real reason. I keep thinking I should feel grateful—he’s healthy, I’m not alone—but the sadness is still right there, dragging everything down.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Yes… it’s happened three, maybe four times this week. Little things set me off—his tiny socks in the laundry, or when he looks up at me and I suddenly feel like I’m failing him. I’ll just sit on the nursery floor with him in my lap and sob, then feel guilty because I’m supposed to be calm for him.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No… I haven’t thought about hurting myself. I do feel overwhelmed and down, but I’ve never pictured doing anything like that.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 25: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Date: ____________  
Patient: Postpartum mother, infant age ___ weeks  

I. Responses Aligned with Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS)  
- EPDS item scores (0–3): Likely 0 on Q10; 2–3 on all other items → provisional total ≈ 26–29 / 30 (indicative range for probable major mood/anxiety disturbance).  

II. Key Symptoms / Behaviors Endorsed  
- Depressed mood, tearfulness most days  
- Marked anhedonia (“nothing’s funny,” “flat”)  
- Excessive inappropriate guilt / self-blame regarding infant care  
- Anxiety: persistent free-floating worry, two recent panic-equivalent episodes  
- Sleep disturbance secondary to rumination, hypervigilance to infant  
- Feeling overwhelmed, “drowning,” task paralysis  
- No self-harm ideation (explicitly denied)  

III. Pattern Summary  
Consistent with moderate–severe postpartum depression with prominent anxiety features; functional impact high (self-care, household tasks, emotional availability).  

IV. Screening Significance & Risk Flags  
- High score range → refer for immediate comprehensive assessment (PHQ-9, GAD-7, EPDS formal scoring)  
- Presence of panic-level arousal → consider co-morbid postpartum anxiety or panic disorder  
- No current self-harm/suicidal ideation; monitor at every contact (safety plan if status changes)  
- Protective factor: strong infant attachment motivation (“push through for the baby”)  

V. Next Steps Documented  
1. Discuss findings with patient; obtain formal EPDS; schedule follow-up within 1 week or sooner if deterioration.  
2. Coordinate referral to perinatal mental health specialist / therapist; consider medication consult.  
3. Provide crisis line numbers; instruct to seek ED if emergent self-harm thoughts develop.
